<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>HOW TO READ YOUR FUND REPORT </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>This report contains information that can help you evaluate your investment. It includes details about your fund&#146;s return and presents data and analysis that provide insight into the fund&#146;s performance and investment approach. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>By reading the letter from Vanguard&#146;s chairman, you&#146;ll get an understanding of how the fund invests and how the market environment affected its performance. The statistical information that follows can help you understand how the fund&#146;s performance and characteristics stack up against those of similar funds and market benchmarks. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>It&#146;s important to keep in mind that any opinions expressed here are just that: informed opinions. They should not be considered promises or advice. These opinions, like the statistics, cover the period through the date on the cover of this report. The risks of investing in the fund are spelled out in the prospectus. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Frequent updates on the fund&#146;s performance and information about some of its holdings are available on Vanguard.com&#174;. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>During the six months ended June 30, 2004, Vanguard 500 Index Fund returned 3.4% as the U.S. stock market traded within a relatively narrow range. Your fund&#146;s return matched the 3.4% return of its benchmark, the Standard &amp; Poor&#146;s 500 Index, and surpassed the 2.0% average return of its peer fund group. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A006></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>STOCKS GAINED AS THE ECONOMY REBOUNDED </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Stock markets worldwide showed moderate gains across the board as investors took heart from a generally positive economic environment. In the United States, corporate earnings were strong, and Wall Street boosted its earnings-growth forecasts as the economic expansion accelerated. Consumer confidence solidified during the half-year as job creation increased. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Gains were tempered, however, by a two-month period in which indicators of rising inflation rattled investors. Unrest in the Middle East and growing global demand pushed the price of oil past a level last seen more than 20 years earlier, during the Iran-Iraq War. But good economic news was back in the headlines in May and June, prompting a snapback for stocks. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=center><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>1 </FONT></P>

<P style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always"></P>

<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 282; page: 282" -->



<HR color=gray noShade SIZE=5>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A007></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Admiral&#153; Shares<BR>A lower-cost class of shares available to many longtime shareholders and to those with significant investments in the fund.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2></FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>For the six months, the broad U.S. stock market, as measured by the Dow Jones Wilshire 5000 Composite Index, returned 3.9%. The Russell 1000 Index of mid- to large-capitalization stocks produced a 3.3% gain, while the Russell 2000 Index, a proxy for small-cap stocks, jumped 6.8%. Across the market-cap spectrum, value-oriented stocks (those that generally trade at below-market valuations relative to their earnings and other fundamental measures) outdistanced growth stocks (those expected to produce above-average earnings growth). </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>European and Pacific markets produced local-currency returns topping those of U.S. stocks. However, international stock returns were dampened somewhat for U.S.-based investors as the rebounding domestic economy and rising interest rates caused the U.S. dollar to strengthen against many currencies. (A stronger U.S. currency means that foreign returns translate into fewer dollars.) Emerging-markets returns, in aggregate, were negative for the six-month period. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A008></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>BONDS REACTED TO THE STRONGER ECONOMY </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>In the fixed income markets, interest rates rose across bond maturities, depressing prices. Rates stayed at historically low levels during the first half of the period, then rose sharply in April as the economy strengthened. For the six months, the yield of the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note increased 33 basis points (0.33 percentage point), from 4.25% to 4.58%. At the short end of the maturity spectrum, rates climbed more sharply in anticipation of the Federal Reserve Board&#146;s increase in its target federal funds rate. The Fed acted on June 30, lifting its target by 25 basis points, the first increase in four years. The yield of the 3-month Treasury bill, a proxy for money market rates, climbed from 0.92% at year-end 2003 to 1.26% on June 30. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>As earnings growth fortified corporate balance sheets, corporate bonds became more attractive, enhancing their performance relative to Treasuries. This trend particularly benefited lesser-quality bonds; the Lehman Brothers High Yield Bond Index, a benchmark of below-investment-grade bonds, posted a six-month return of 1.4%, compared with the 0.2% return of the broad market, as measured by the Lehman Aggregate Bond Index. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=center><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>2 </FONT></P>

<P style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always"></P>

<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 283; page: 283" -->



<HR color=gray noShade SIZE=5>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A009></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>THE FUND&#146;S PERFORMANCE WAS RELATIVELY PLACID </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Consistent with the relatively narrow trading ranges that the U.S. stock market experienced during the first half of 2004, Vanguard 500 Index Fund quietly tacked its way to a 3.4% gain, closely following the S&amp;P 500 Index. At the beginning of the year, the fund was still riding the momentum of last year&#146;s 28.5% gain, and by early March it had advanced an additional 4.3%. However, investor sentiment then cooled, and the fund backtracked to end the first quarter with a 1.7% gain. The second quarter was similarly indecisive, with a mildly up-and-down pattern that ended with another three-month increase of 1.7%. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>During the six-month period, higher energy prices and improved earnings fueled a rally in the integrated oils sector. These big oil companies, including ExxonMobil, ChevronTexaco, and ConocoPhillips, collectively rose about 11%. The &#147;other energy&#148; companies, which typically focus on specialized aspects of oil and natural gas exploration, production, and related products and services, advanced about 17%. Taken together, these two energy-related sectors were the leading engine for Vanguard 500 Index Fund&#146;s gain. </FONT></P>

<PRE>
- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The &#147;other&#148; sector, which includes conglomerates such as General Electric and 3M, was another standout, returning more than 8%. The consumer discretionary group&#151;mostly retailers, media, and entertainment companies&#151;benefited from healthy consumer spending and therefore also performed better than average, gaining about 5%. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Among the sectors that turned in substandard performances was the fund&#146;s largest, financial services, which is typically vulnerable to rising interest rates. It advanced in the neighborhood of 2%. The only sector to lose ground was technology, the fund&#146;s second-largest, which cooled off after a sizzling 2003 and declined by less than 1%. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=center><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>3 </FONT></P>

<P style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always"></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A010></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>THE ENDURING BENEFITS OF INDEX INVESTING </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Investing in the stock market is often compared with riding a roller coaster. Since 1995, that analogy has been particularly apt, with the overall U.S. market delivering double-digit gains in six different calendar years and double-digit losses in three others. Thus far in 2004, Vanguard 500 Index Fund, like its benchmark, has changed the tempo by gliding more than gyrating. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Of course, no one knows for sure whether the ride for the rest of 2004 and beyond will be smooth or dizzying. That&#146;s why we encourage all our shareholders to continue to evaluate investments from a long-term perspective. The march of time smoothes out short-term patterns and, based on history, rewards patience. And investing in an index fund such as Vanguard 500 Index Fund is an ideal way to capitalize on the stock market&#146;s long-term potential. Because the fund holds all 500 stocks that make up the S&amp;P 500, your investment is broad-based and well positioned to benefit from any gains that the U.S. economy generates in the future. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>In fact, your fund&#146;s characteristics of diversification, low turnover, and low costs constitute a model for managing all your investments. We&#146;re more convinced than ever that your best plan for long-term success is to maintain a steady, diversified mix of low-cost stock, bond, and cash investments tailored to your situation. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>We appreciate your continued confidence in Vanguard, and we look forward to reporting to you in early 2005. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A016></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>GLOSSARY OF INVESTMENT TERMS </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>BETA.</B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; A measure of the magnitude of a fund&#146;s past share-price fluctuations in relation to the ups and downs of a given market index. The index is assigned a beta of 1.00. Compared with a given index, a fund with a beta of 1.20 typically would have seen its share price rise or fall by 12% when the index rose or fell by 10%. A fund&#146;s beta should be reviewed in conjunction with its R-squared (see definition below). The lower the R-squared, the less correlation there is between the fund and the index, and the less reliable beta is as an indicator of volatility.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>EARNINGS GROWTH RATE.</B> The average annual rate of growth in earnings over the past five years for the stocks now in a fund. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>EXPENSE RATIO.</B> The percentage of a fund&#146;s average net assets used to pay its annual administrative and advisory expenses. These expenses directly reduce returns to investors. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>FOREIGN HOLDINGS.</B> The percentage of a fund&#146;s equity assets represented by stocks or depositary receipts of companies based outside the United States. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>MEDIAN MARKET CAP</B>. An indicator of the size of companies in which a fund invests; the midpoint of market capitalization (market price x shares outstanding) of a fund&#146;s stocks, weighted by the proportion of the fund&#146;s assets invested in each stock. Stocks representing half of the fund&#146;s assets have market capitalizations above the median, and the rest are below it. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>PRICE/BOOK RATIO.</B> The share price of a stock divided by its net worth, or book value, per share. For a fund, the weighted average price/book ratio of the stocks it holds. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>PRICE/EARNINGS RATIO.</B> The ratio of a stock&#146;s current price to its per-share earnings over the past year. For a fund, the weighted average P/E of the stocks it holds. P/E is an indicator of market expectations about corporate prospects; the higher the P/E, the greater the expectations for a company&#146;s future growth. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>R-SQUARED.</B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; A measure of how much of a fund&#146;s past returns can be explained by the returns from the market in general, as measured by a given index. If a fund&#146;s total returns were precisely synchronized with an index&#146;s returns, its R-squared would be 1.00. If the fund&#146;s returns bore no relationship to the index&#146;s returns, its R-squared would be 0.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>RETURN ON EQUITY.</B> The annual average rate of return generated by a company during the past five years for each dollar of shareholder&#146;s equity (net income divided by shareholder&#146;s equity). For a fund, the weighted average return on equity for the companies whose stocks it holds. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>SHORT-TERM RESERVES.</B> The percentage of a fund invested in highly liquid, short-term securities that can be readily converted to cash. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>TURNOVER RATE.</B> An indication of the fund&#146;s trading activity. Funds with high turnover rates incur higher transaction costs and may be more likely to distribute capital gains (which may be taxable to investors). </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>YIELD.</B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; A snapshot of a fund&#146;s income from interest and dividends. The yield, expressed as a percentage of the fund&#146;s net asset value, is based on income earned over the past 30 days and is annualized, or projected forward for the coming year. The index yield is based on the current annualized rate of income provided by securities in the index.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->

<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>ABOUT YOUR FUND&#146;S EXPENSES </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>We believe it is important for you to understand the impact of costs on your investment. All mutual funds have operating expenses. As a shareholder of the fund, you incur ongoing costs, which include costs for portfolio management, administrative services, and shareholder reports (like this one), among others. Operating expenses, which are deducted from a fund&#146;s gross income, directly reduce the investment return of the fund. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>A fund&#146;s expenses are expressed as a percentage of its average net assets. This figure is known as the expense ratio. The following examples are intended to help you understand the ongoing costs (in dollars) of investing in your fund and to compare these costs with those of other mutual funds. The examples are based on an investment of $1,000 made at the beginning of the period shown and held for the entire period. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The table below illustrates your fund&#146;s costs in two ways: </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>&#149; <B>ACTUAL FUND RETURN.</B> This section helps you to estimate the actual expenses that you paid over the period. The &#147;Ending Account Value&#148; shown is derived from the fund&#146;s actual return, and the third column shows the dollar amount that would have been paid by an investor who started with $1,000 in the fund. You may use the information here, together with the amount you invested, to estimate the expenses that you paid over the period. To do so, simply divide your account value by $1,000 (for example, an $8,600 account value divided by $1,000 = 8.6), then multiply the result by the number given for your fund under the heading &#147;Expenses Paid During Period.&#148; </FONT></P>

<A name=A019></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>STATEMENT OF NET ASSETS </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>This Statement provides a detailed list of the fund&#146;s holdings, including each security&#146;s market value on the last day of the reporting period. Securities are grouped and subtotaled by asset type (common stocks, bonds, etc.) and by industry sector. Other assets are added to, and liabilities are subtracted from, the value of <I>Total Investments</I> to calculate the fund&#146;s <I>Net Assets</I>. Finally, <I>Net Assets</I> are divided by the outstanding shares of the fund to arrive at its share price, or <I>Net Asset Value (NAV)</I> Per Share. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>At the end of the Statement of Net Assets, you will find a table displaying the composition of the fund&#146;s net assets. Because all income and any realized gains must be distributed to shareholders each year, the bulk of net assets consists of <I>Paid-in Capital</I> (money invested by shareholders). The amounts shown for <I>Undistributed Net Investment Income</I> and <I>Accumulated Net Realized Gains</I> usually approximate the sums the fund had available to distribute to shareholders as income dividends or capital gains as of the statement date, but may differ because certain investments or transactions may be treated differently for financial statement and tax purposes. Any <I>Accumulated Net Realized Losses,</I> and any cumulative excess of distributions over net income or net realized gains, will appear as negative balances. <I>Unrealized Appreciation (Depreciation)</I> is the difference between the market value of the fund&#146;s investments
and their cost, and reflects the gains (losses) that would be realized if the fund were to sell all of its investments at their statement-date values. </FONT></P>

<A name=A023></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Vanguard 500 Index Fund is registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 as an open-end investment company, or mutual fund. The fund offers two classes of shares, Investor Shares and Admiral Shares. Investor Shares are available to any investor who meets the fund&#146;s minimum purchase requirements. Admiral Shares are designed for investors who meet certain administrative, servicing, tenure, and account-size criteria. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>A.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The following significant accounting policies conform to generally accepted accounting principles for U.S. mutual funds. The fund consistently follows such policies in preparing its financial statements.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>1.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <B>Security Valuation:</B> Securities are valued as of the close of trading on the New York Stock Exchange (generally 4:00 p.m. Eastern time) on the valuation date. Equity securities are valued at the latest quoted sales prices or official closing prices taken from the primary market in which each security trades; such securities not traded on the valuation date are valued at the mean of the latest quoted bid and asked prices. Securities for which market quotations are not readily available, or whose values have been materially affected by events occurring before the fund&#146;s pricing time but after the close of the securities&#146; primary markets, are valued by methods deemed by the board of trustees to represent fair value. Temporary cash investments acquired over 60 days to maturity are valued using the latest bid prices or using valuations based on a matrix system (which considers such factors as security prices,
yields, maturities, and ratings), both as furnished by independent pricing services. Other temporary cash investments are valued at amortized cost, which approximates market value.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>2.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <B>Futures Contracts:</B> The fund uses S&amp;P 500 Index futures contracts to a limited extent, with the objectives of maintaining full exposure to the stock market, enhancing returns, maintaining liquidity, and minimizing transaction costs. The fund may purchase futures contracts to immediately invest incoming cash in the market, or sell futures in response to cash outflows, thereby simulating a fully invested position in the underlying index while maintaining a cash balance for liquidity. The fund may seek to enhance returns by using futures contracts instead of the underlying securities when futures are believed to be priced more attractively than the underlying securities. The primary risks associated with the use of futures contracts are imperfect correlation between changes in market values of stocks held by the fund and the prices of futures contracts, and the possibility of an illiquid market. Futures contracts are
valued at their quoted daily settlement prices. The aggregate principal amounts of the contracts are not recorded in the financial statements. Fluctuations in the value of the contracts are recorded in the Statement of Net Assets as an asset (liability) and in the Statement of Operations as unrealized appreciation (depreciation) until the contracts are closed, when they are recorded as realized futures gains (losses).</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>3.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <B>Repurchase Agreements:</B> The fund, along with other members of The Vanguard Group, transfers uninvested cash balances to a pooled cash account, which is invested in repurchase agreements secured by U.S. government securities. Securities pledged as collateral for repurchase agreements are held by a custodian bank until the agreements mature. Each agreement requires that the market value of the collateral be sufficient to cover payments of interest and principal; however, in the event of default or bankruptcy by the other party to the agreement, retention of the collateral may be subject to legal proceedings.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>4.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <B>Federal Income Taxes:</B> The fund intends to continue to qualify as a regulated investment company and distribute all of its taxable income. Accordingly, no provision for federal income taxes is required in the financial statements.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>5.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <B>Distributions:</B> Distributions to shareholders are recorded on the ex-dividend date.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=center><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>22 </FONT></P>

<P style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always"></P>

<!-- MARKER PAGE="sheet: 303; page: 303" -->



<HR color=gray noShade SIZE=5>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>6.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; <B>Other:</B> Dividend income is recorded on the ex-dividend date. Security transactions are accounted for on the date securities are bought or sold. Costs used to determine realized gains (losses) on the sale of investment securities are those of the specific securities sold.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Each class of shares has equal rights as to assets and earnings, except that each class separately bears certain class-specific expenses related to maintenance of shareholder accounts (included in Management and Administrative expenses) and shareholder reporting. Marketing and distribution expenses are allocated to each class of shares based on a method approved by the board of trustees. Income, other non-class-specific expenses, and realized and unrealized gains and losses on investments are allocated to each class of shares based on its relative net assets. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>B.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Vanguard Group furnishes at cost investment advisory, corporate management, administrative, marketing, and distribution services. The costs of such services are allocated to the fund under methods approved by the board of trustees. The fund has committed to provide up to 0.40% of its net assets in capital contributions to Vanguard. At June 30, 2004, the fund had contributed capital of $14,232,000 to Vanguard (included in Other Assets), representing 0.01% of the fund&#146;s net assets and 14.23% of Vanguard&#146;s capitalization. The fund&#146;s trustees and officers are also directors and officers of Vanguard.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>C.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Distributions are determined on a tax basis and may differ from net investment income and realized capital gains for financial reporting purposes. Differences may be permanent or temporary. Permanent differences are reclassified among capital accounts in the financial statements to reflect their tax character. Temporary differences arise when certain items of income, expense, gain, or loss are recognized in different periods for financial statement and tax purposes; these differences will reverse at some time in the future. Differences in classification may also result from the treatment of short-term gains as ordinary income for tax purposes.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>During the six months ended June 30, 2004, the fund realized $241,353,000 of net capital gains resulting from in-kind redemptions&#151;in which shareholders exchange fund shares for securities held by the fund rather than for cash. Because such gains are not taxable to the fund, and are not distributed to shareholders, they have been reclassified from accumulated net realized gains to paid-in capital. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The fund&#146;s tax-basis capital gains and losses are determined only at the end of each fiscal year. For tax purposes, at December 31, 2003, the fund had available realized losses of $4,349,644,000 to offset future net capital gains of $193,358,000 through December 31, 2008, $890,248,000 through December 31, 2009, $3,087,963,000 through December 31, 2010, $176,196,000 through December 31, 2011, and $1,879,000 through December 31, 2012. The fund will use these capital losses to offset net taxable capital gains, if any, realized during the year ending December 31, 2004; should the fund realize net capital losses for the year, the losses will be added to the loss carry forward balances above. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>At June 30, 2004, net unrealized appreciation of investment securities for tax purposes was $23,384,797,000, consisting of unrealized gains of $31,452,832,000 on securities that had risen in value since their purchase and $8,068,035,000 in unrealized losses on securities that had fallen in value since their purchase. </FONT></P>

<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (CONTINUED) </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>At June 30, 2004, the aggregate settlement value of open futures contracts expiring in September 2004 and the related unrealized appreciation (depreciation) were: </FONT></P>

<PRE>
- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

<A name=A027></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>CAPITALIZE ON YOUR IRA </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Are you taking full advantage of your individual retirement account? You really should be. These tax-deferred accounts are powerful options for retirement savers. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Here&#146;s how you can exploit your IRA&#151;and improve your chances of having the retirement of your dreams. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A028></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>CONTRIBUTE THE MAXIMUM AMOUNT EACH YEAR </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>It may be an obvious point, but if you invest as much in your IRA as the law allows&#151;currently $3,000 per tax year if you are under age 50 and $3,500 if you are age 50 or over&#151;you will increase the odds of meeting your retirement goals. &#147;Max out&#148; every year you can. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A029></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>MAKE IT AUTOMATIC </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Put your IRA on autopilot by taking advantage of Vanguard&#146;s Automatic Investment Plan. Your IRA contributions will be deducted from your bank account on a schedule of your choosing, making retirement investing a healthy habit. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A030></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>CONSIDER COST </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The owners of low-cost investments keep a larger portion of their gross returns than the owners of high-cost investments. Over the long term, avoiding costlier mutual funds and brokerage commissions could significantly boost your retirement savings. Our low costs are one reason a Vanguard IRA&#174; is such a smart choice. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<A name=A031></A>
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>REQUEST A DIRECT ROLLOVER WHEN YOU CHANGE JOBS </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Don&#146;t spend your retirement assets before you&#146;ve retired. When you change jobs, roll your 401(k) or other employer-sponsored retirement plan assets directly into your IRA. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<H1 align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Summary </FONT></H1>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2> Stock gains were fairly strong during the first three months of 2004, but they became more subdued in the April&#150;June quarter as investors weighed the effects of rising interest rates and inflation. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2> During the half-year, the Investor Shares of Vanguard&#146;s three small-capitalization index funds posted gains that ranged from 7.2% to 8.1%. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2> Small-cap stocks led the market. Value stocks generally outpaced growth issues. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Want less clutter in your mailbox? Just register with Vanguard.com and opt to get fund reports online.</B> </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Major Left Bold-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<HR color=gray noShade SIZE=5>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>LETTER FROM THE CHAIRMAN </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Fellow Shareholder, </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The impressive rebound of small-capitalization stocks that began in 2003 continued into the first quarter of this year, then slowed notably during the second quarter. For the first six months of 2004, the Investor Shares of Vanguard Small-Cap Index Fund, Small-Cap Growth Index Fund, and Small-Cap Value Index Fund posted returns of 7.7%, 7.2%, and 8.1%, respectively. </FONT></P>
<IMG src="jb_a.gif"> <IMG src="jb_b.gif"> <IMG src="jb_c.gif">
<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>All three funds satisfied their objective of closely tracking their respective indexes. Two of the three&#151;the Small-Cap Index Fund and the Small-Cap Growth Index Fund&#151;also outperformed their peer-group averages, while the Small-Cap Value Index Fund was just a fraction shy. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The table on the following page shows the total returns for the funds&#146; share classes, their target indexes, and their average mutual fund peers. The funds&#146; starting and ending share prices are shown on page 5; there were no distributions to shareholders during the six months. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>STOCKS GAINED AS THE ECONOMY REBOUNDED </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Stock markets worldwide showed moderate gains across the board as investors took heart from a generally positive economic environment. In the United States, corporate earnings were strong, and Wall Street boosted its earnings-growth forecasts as the economic expansion accelerated. Consumer confidence solidified during the half-year as job creation increased. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Gains were tempered, however, by a two-month period in which indicators of rising inflation rattled investors. Unrest in the Middle East and growing global demand pushed the price of crude oil past a level last seen more than 20 years earlier, during the Iran-Iraq War. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=center><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>1 </FONT></P>

<P style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always"></P>

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>But good economic news was back in the headlines in May and June, prompting a snapback for stocks. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>For the six months, the broad U.S. stock market, as measured by the Dow Jones Wilshire 5000 Composite Index, returned 3.9%. Across the market-cap spectrum, value-oriented stocks (those that generally trade at below-market valuations relative to their earnings and other fundamental measures) outdistanced growth stocks (those expected to produce above-average earnings growth). </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>European and Pacific markets produced local-currency returns topping those of U.S. stocks. However, international stock returns were dampened somewhat for U.S.-based investors as the rebounding domestic economy and rising interest rates caused the U.S. dollar to strengthen against many currencies. (A stronger U.S. currency means that foreign returns translate into fewer dollars.) Emerging-markets returns, in the aggregate, were negative for the six-month period. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>BONDS REACTED TO THE STRONGER ECONOMY </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>In the fixed income markets, interest rates rose across bond maturities, depressing prices. Rates stayed at historically low levels during the first half of the period, then rose sharply in April as the economy strengthened. For the six months, the yield of the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note increased 33 basis points (0.33 percentage point), from 4.25% to 4.58%. At the short end of the maturity spectrum, rates climbed more sharply in anticipation of the Federal Reserve Board&#146;s increase in its target federal funds rate. The Fed acted on </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=center><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>2 </FONT></P>

<P style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always"></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Major Left Bold-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<H1 align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Admiral&#153; Shares </FONT></H1>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>A lower-cost class of shares available to many longtime shareholders and to those with significant investments in the fund.</B> </FONT></P>

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>June 30, lifting its target by 25 basis points, the first increase in four years. The yield of the 3-month Treasury bill, a proxy for money market rates, climbed from 0.92% at year-end 2003 to 1.26% on June 30. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>As earnings growth fortified corporate balance sheets, corporate bonds became more attractive, enhancing their performance relative to Treasuries. This trend particularly benefited lower-quality bonds; the Lehman Brothers High Yield Bond Index, a benchmark of below-investment-grade bonds, posted a six-month return of 1.4%, compared with the 0.2% return of the broad market, as measured by the Lehman Aggregate Bond Index. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>SMALLER STOCKS WERE THE MARKET&#146;S LEADERS </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Small-cap stocks continued to prove their resilience in the first half of 2004, topping the returns of both mid- and large-capitalization issues. Within Vanguard&#146;s three small-cap index funds, most industry sectors saw gains. As is typically true, the return of the Small-Cap Index Fund, which includes stocks of both the growth and value ilk, was roughly midway between the returns for the style-based funds. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Most of the Small-Cap Index Fund&#146;s 7.7% half-year return was earned in the first three months, before the second-quarter slowdown took hold in the market. Leading the target index were several sectors&#151;including &#147;other energy,&#148; health care, producer durables, consumer discretionary, and materials &amp; processing&#151;that provided generous contributions to the overall return. Technology issues, the &#147;hottest&#148; sector of the previous year, turned in the poorest results, plagued by both global competition and a feeling among some investors that tech stocks had gotten too pricey. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>In the Small-Cap Growth Index Fund, consumer discretionary issues and &#147;other energy&#148; stocks&#151;largely exploration, production, and service- </FONT></P>

<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>CHOOSE YOUR COURSE AND STICK TO IT </FONT></P>

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The financial markets can be very difficult to navigate. Indeed, their ups and downs can make the process of reaching your goals seem indirect at best. But, as we have advised investors for years, the most productive response to this uncertainty is to have reasonable expectations and to maintain a balanced portfolio that meets your needs and risk tolerance. Over the long run, a prudent, balanced approach allows you to participate in the markets&#146; gains while cushioning the effects of the markets&#146; darker days. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Major Left Bold-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<H1 align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>GLOSSARY OF INVESTMENT TERMS </FONT></H1>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Beta.</B> A measure of the magnitude of a fund's past share-price fluctuations in relation to the ups and downs of a given market index. The index is assigned a beta of 1.00. Compared with a given index, a fund with a beta of 1.20 typically would have seen its share price rise or fall by 12% when the index rose or fell by 10%. A fund's beta should be reviewed in conjunction with its R-squared (see definition below). The lower the R-squared, the less correlation there is between the fund and the index, and the less reliable beta is as an indicator of volatility. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Earnings Growth Rate.</B> The average annual rate of growth in earnings over the past five years for the stocks now in a fund. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Expense Ratio.</B> The percentage of a fund's average net assets used to pay its annual administrative and advisory expenses. These expenses directly reduce returns to investors. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Foreign Holdings.</B> The percentage of a fund's equity assets represented by stocks or depositary receipts of companies based outside the United States. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Median Market Cap.</B> An indicator of the size of companies in which a fund invests; the midpoint of market capitalization (market price x shares outstanding) of a fund's stocks, weighted by the proportion of the fund's assets invested in each stock. Stocks representing half of the fund's assets have market capitalizations above the median, and the rest are below it. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Price/Book Ratio.</B> The share price of a stock divided by its net worth, or book value, per share. For a fund, the weighted average price/book ratio of the stocks it holds. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Price/Earnings Ratio.</B> The ratio of a stock's current price to its per-share earnings over the past year. For a fund, the weighted average P/E of the stocks it holds. P/E is an indicator of market expectations about corporate prospects; the higher the P/E, the greater the expectations for a company's future growth. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>R-Squared.</B> A measure of how much of a fund's past returns can be explained by the returns from the market in general, as measured by a given index. If a fund's total returns were precisely synchronized with an index's returns, its R-squared would be 1.00. If the fund's returns bore no relationship to the index's returns, its R-squared would be 0. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Return on Equity.</B> The annual average rate of return generated by a company during the past five years for each dollar of shareholder's equity (net income divided by shareholder's equity). For a fund, the weighted average return on equity for the companies whose stocks it holds. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Short-Term Reserves.</B> The percentage of a fund invested in highly liquid, short-term securities that can be readily converted to cash. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Turnover Rate.</B> An indication of the fund's trading activity. Funds with high turnover rates incur higher transaction costs and may be more likely to distribute capital gains (which may be taxable to investors). </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>Yield.</B> A snapshot of a fund's income from interest and dividends. The yield, expressed as a percentage of the fund's net asset value, is based on income earned over the past 30 days and is annualized, or projected forward for the coming year. The index yield is based on the current annualized rate of income provided by securities in the index. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=center><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>10 </FONT></P>

<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>ABOUT YOUR FUND&#146;S EXPENSES </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>We believe it is important for you to understand the impact of costs on your investment. All mutual funds have operating expenses. As a shareholder of the fund, you incur ongoing costs, which include costs for portfolio management, administrative services, and shareholder reports (like this one), among others. Operating expenses, which are deducted from a fund&#146;s gross income, directly reduce the investment return of the fund. A fund&#146;s expenses are expressed as a percentage of its average net assets. This figure is known as the expense ratio. The following examples are intended to help you understand the ongoing costs (in dollars) of investing in your fund and to compare these costs with those of other mutual funds. The examples are based on an investment of $1,000 made at the beginning of the period shown and held for the entire period. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>&#149;Actual fund return. </B>This section helps you to estimate the actual expenses that you paid over the period. The &#147;Ending Account Value&#148; shown is derived from the fund&#146;s actual return, and the third column shows the dollar amount that would have been paid by an investor who started with $1,000 in the fund. You may use the information here, together with the amount you invested, to estimate the expenses that you paid over the period. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>To do so, simply divide your account value by $1,000 (for example, an $8,600 account value divided by $1,000 = 8.6), then multiply the result by the number given for your fund under the heading &#147;Expenses Paid During Period.&#148; </FONT></P>

Your fund does not charge transaction fees, such as purchase or redemption fees, nor does it carry a &#147;sales load.&#148; The calculations assume no shares were bought or sold during the period. Your actual costs may have been higher or lower, depending on the amount of your investment and the timing of any purchases or redemptions. You can find more information about the fund&#146;s expenses, including annual expense ratios for the past five years, in the Financial Statements section of this report. For additional information on operating expenses and other shareholder costs, please refer to the

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>As of 6/30/2004 </B><BR>FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (UNAUDITED)<BR>STATEMENT OF NET ASSETS<BR>This Statement provides a detailed list of each fund&#146;s holdings, including each security&#146;s market value on the last day of the reporting period. Securities are grouped and subtotaled by asset type (common stocks, bonds, etc.) and by industry sector. Other assets are added to, and liabilities are subtracted from, the value of <I>Total Investments </I>to calculate the fund&#146;s <I>Net Assets</I>. Finally, <I>Net Assets </I>are divided by the outstanding shares of the fund to arrive at its share price, or <I>Net Asset Value (NAV) Per Share</I>. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>At the end of the Statement of Net Assets, you will find a table displaying the composition of the fund&#146;s net assets. Because all income and any realized gains must be distributed to shareholders each year, the bulk of net assets consists of <I>Paid-in Capital </I>(money invested by shareholders). The amounts shown for <I>Undistributed Net Investment Income </I>and <I>Accumulated Net Realized Gains </I>usually approximate the sums the fund had available to distribute to shareholders as income dividends or capital gains as of the statement date, but may differ because certain investments or transactions may be treated differently for financial statement and tax purposes. Any <I>Accumulated Net Realized Losses</I>, and any cumulative excess of distributions over net income or net realized gains, will appear as negative balances. <I>Unrealized Appreciation (Depreciation) </I>is the difference between the market value of the fund&#146;s investments
and their cost, and reflects the gains (losses) that would be realized if the fund were to sell all of its investments at their statement-date values. </FONT></P>

<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Vanguard Small-Cap Index, Small-Cap Growth Index, and Small-Cap Value Index Funds are registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 as open-end investment companies, or mutual funds. The Small-Cap Index Fund offers four classes of shares: Investor Shares, Admiral Shares, Institutional Shares, and VIPER Shares. The Small-Cap Growth Index and Small-Cap Value Index Funds each offer three classes of shares, Investor Shares, Institutional Shares, and VIPER Shares. Investor Shares are available to any investor who meets the fund&#146;s minimum purchase requirements. Admiral Shares are designed for investors who meet certain administrative, servicing, tenure, and account-size criteria. Institutional Shares are designed for investors who meet certain administrative and servicing criteria and invest a minimum of $10 million. VIPER Shares are listed for trading on the American Stock Exchange; they can be purchased and sold through a broker. The Small-Cap
Index, Small-Cap Growth Index, and Small-Cap Value Index Funds VIPER Shares were first issued on January 26, 2004, and offered to the public on January 30, 2004. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>A</B>.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The following significant accounting policies conform to generally accepted accounting principles for U.S. mutual funds. The funds consistently follow such policies in preparing their financial statements.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>1.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Security Valuation: </B>Securities are valued as of the close of trading on the New York Stock Exchange (generally 4:00 p.m. Eastern time) on the valuation date. Equity securities are valued at the latest quoted sales prices or official closing prices taken from the primary market in which each security trades; such securities not traded on the valuation date are valued at the mean of the latest quoted bid and asked prices. Securities for which market quotations are not readily available, or whose values have been materially affected by events occurring before the funds&#146; pricing time but after the close of the securities&#146; primary markets, are valued by methods deemed by the board of trustees to represent fair value. Temporary cash investments acquired over 60 days to maturity are valued using the latest bid prices or using valuations based on a matrix system (which considers such factors as security prices,
yields, maturities, and ratings), both as furnished by independent pricing services. Other temporary cash investments are valued at amortized cost, which approximates market value.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>2.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Futures Contracts: </B>The funds use Russell 2000 Index and S&amp;P MidCap 400 Index futures contracts to a limited extent, with the objectives of maintaining full exposure to the stock market, enhancing returns, maintaining liquidity, and minimizing transaction costs. A fund may purchase futures contracts to immediately invest incoming cash in the market, or sell futures in response to cash outflows, thereby simulating a fully invested position in the underlying index while maintaining a cash balance for liquidity. A fund may seek to enhance returns by using futures contracts instead of the underlying securities when futures are believed to be priced more attractively than the underlying securities. The primary risks associated with the use of futures contracts are imperfect correlation between changes in market values of stocks held by the fund and the prices of futures contracts, and the possibility of an illiquid
market.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Futures contracts are valued at their quoted daily settlement prices. The aggregate principal amounts of the contracts are not recorded in the financial statements. Fluctuations in the value of the contracts are recorded in the Statement of Net Assets as an asset (liability) and in the Statement of Operations as unrealized appreciation (depreciation) until the contracts are closed, when they are recorded as realized futures gains (losses). </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>3.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Repurchase Agreements: </B>The funds, along with other members of The Vanguard Group, transfer uninvested cash balances to a pooled cash account, which is invested in repurchase agreements secured by U.S. government securities. Securities pledged as collateral for repurchase agreements are held by a custodian bank until the agreements mature. Each agreement requires that the market value of the collateral be sufficient to cover payments of interest and principal; however, in the event of default or bankruptcy by the other party to the agreement, retention of the collateral may be subject to legal proceedings.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Page Number Center" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=center><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>73 </FONT></P>

<P style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always"></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>4.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Federal Income Taxes: </B>Each fund intends to continue to qualify as a regulated investment company and distribute all of its taxable income. Accordingly, no provision for federal income taxes is required in the financial statements.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>5.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Distributions: </B>Distributions to shareholders are recorded on the ex-dividend date.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>6.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Other: </B>Dividend income is recorded on the ex-dividend date. Security transactions are accounted for on the date securities are bought or sold. Costs used to determine realized gains (losses) on the sale of investment securities are those of the specific securities sold.</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Each class of shares has equal rights as to assets and earnings, except that each class separately bears certain class-specific expenses related to maintenance of shareholder accounts (included in Management and Administrative expenses) and shareholder reporting. Marketing and distribution expenses are allocated to each class of shares based on a method approved by the board of trustees. Income, other non-class-specific expenses, and gains and losses on investments are allocated to each class of shares based on its relative net assets. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>B.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; </B>The Vanguard Group furnishes at cost investment advisory, corporate management, administrative, marketing, and distribution services. The costs of such services are allocated to each fund under methods approved by the board of trustees. Each fund has committed to provide up to 0.40% of its net assets in capital contributions to Vanguard. At June 30, 2004, the funds had contributed capital to Vanguard (included in Other Assets) of:</FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para (List) Flush Lv 0- Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2><B>C.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; </B>Distributions are determined on a tax basis and may differ from net investment income and realized capital gains for financial reporting purposes. Differences may be permanent or temporary. Permanent differences are reclassified among capital accounts in the financial statements to reflect their tax character. Temporary differences arise when certain items of income, expense, gain, or loss are recognized in different periods for financial statement and tax purposes; these differences will reverse at some time in the future. Differences in classification may also result from the treatment of short-term gains as ordinary income for tax purposes.</FONT></P>

Because such gains are not taxable to the funds, and are not distributed to shareholders, they have been reclassified from accumulated net realized gains to paid-in capital. </FONT></P>

<H1 align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>CAPITALIZE ON YOUR IRA </FONT></H1>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Here&#146;s how you can exploit your IRA&#151;and improve your chances of having the retirement of your dreams. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>CONTRIBUTE THE MAXIMUM AMOUNT EACH YEAR </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>It may be an obvious point, but if you invest as much in your IRA as the law allows&#151;currently $3,000 per tax year if you are under age 50 and $3,500 if you are age 50 or over&#151;you will increase the odds of meeting your retirement goals. &#147;Max out&#148; every year you can. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>MAKE IT AUTOMATIC </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Put your IRA on autopilot by taking advantage of Vanguard&#146;s Automatic Investment Plan. Your IRA contributions will be deducted from your bank account on a schedule of your choosing, making retirement investing a healthy habit. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>CONSIDER COST </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The owners of low-cost investments keep a larger portion of their gross returns than the owners of high-cost investments. Over the long term, avoiding costlier mutual funds and brokerage commissions could significantly boost your retirement savings. Our low costs are one reason a Vanguard IRA&#174; is such a smart choice. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>REQUEST A DIRECT ROLLOVER WHEN YOU CHANGE JOBS </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Don&#146;t spend your retirement assets before you&#146;ve retired. When you change jobs, roll your 401(k) or other employer-sponsored retirement plan assets directly into your IRA. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>the economic expansion accelerated. Consumer confidence solidified during the half-year as job creation increased. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>Gains were tempered, however, by a two-month period in which indicators of rising inflation rattled investors. Unrest in the Middle East and growing global demand pushed the price of crude oil past a level last seen more than 20 years earlier, during the Iran-Iraq War. But good economic news was back in the headlines in May and June, prompting a snapback for stocks. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>For the six months, the broad U.S. stock market, as measured by the Dow Jones Wilshire 5000 Composite Index, returned 3.9%. The Russell 1000 Index of mid- to large-cap stocks produced a 3.3% gain, while the Russell 2000 Index, a proxy for small-cap stocks, jumped 6.8%. Across the market-cap spectrum, value-oriented stocks (those that generally trade at below-market valuations relative to their earnings and other fundamental measures) outdistanced growth stocks (those expected to produce above-average earnings growth). </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>European and Pacific markets produced local-currency returns topping those of U.S. stocks. However, international stock returns were dampened somewhat for U.S.-based investors as the rebounding domestic economy and rising interest rates caused the U.S. dollar to strengthen against many currencies. (A stronger U.S. currency means that foreign returns translate into fewer dollars.) Emerging-markets returns, in the aggregate, were negative for the six-month period. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>In the fixed income markets, interest rates rose across bond maturities, depressing prices. Rates stayed at historically low levels during the first half of the period, then rose sharply in April as the economy strengthened. For the six months, the yield of the benchmark 10-year U.S. </FONT></P>

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>As earnings growth fortified corporate balance sheets, corporate bonds became more attractive, enhancing their performance relative to Treasuries. This trend particularly benefited lower-quality bonds; the Lehman Brothers High Yield Bond Index, a benchmark of below-investment-grade bonds, posted a six-month return of 1.4%, compared with the 0.2% return of the broad market, as measured by the Lehman Aggregate Bond Index. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Head Left-Arial" FSL="Project" -->
<P align=left><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>THE FUND&#146;S MID-CAP HOLDINGS DID WELL </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Project" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The six-month results for both funds were very good, and both funds satisfied their respective objectives of closely tracking their target benchmarks&#146; returns. The 6.0% return of the Extended Market Index Fund&#146;s Investor Shares was marginally higher than the 5.8% return of the unmanaged Dow Jones Wilshire 4500 Completion Index, while the 5.8% return of the Mid-Cap Index Fund&#146;s Investor Shares slightly lagged the 5.9% return of the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) US Mid Cap 450 Index. While both funds scored solid gains in the first quarter, their results in the second quarter were significantly lower, owing to higher energy prices, rising interest rates, and ongoing geopolitical tensions&#151;factors that affected stocks of all market capitalizations. </FONT></P>

<!-- MARKER FORMAT-SHEET="Para Flush Lv 0-Arial" FSL="Default" -->

<P><FONT face="Arial, Helvetica, Sans-Serif" size=2>The Extended Market Index Fund drew positive returns from 10 of its 12 constituent sectors. The fund had a competitive advantage over its </FONT></P>

The strongest result was in the &#147;other energy&#148; sector&#151;made up of companies that provide exploration, research, and other services to oil companies&#151;which had a six-month return of almost 23%. Many consumer-oriented stocks that tend to perform well during economic rebounds also produced beneficial returns. The consumer staples and consumer discretionary sectors added 0.3 and 1.6 percentage points, respectively, to the fund&#146;s Investor Shares&#146; 6.0% return. Stock gains in the health care and materials &amp; processing groups also bolstered the fund&#146;s return. The fund&#146;s holdings in the economically sensitive financial services sector (the fund&#146;s largest sector holding) and in the utilities sector were understandable disappointments in the rising-rate
environment. Technology stocks suffered losses as global competition and overvaluations were cited as reasons for poor performances. </FONT></P>

The best showing was the 30% return posted by large integrated-oils companies, a gain driven by rising oil prices and global demand. As was the case for the Extended Market Index Fund, the consumer staples and consumer discretionary industry groups were among the leading contributors, adding 0.5 and 1.4 percentage points, respectively, to the fund&#146;s return. Several other sectors, including materials &amp; processing, &#147;other energy,&#148; and utilities, also posted index-beating returns that added to the fund&#146;s return. Again, technology was the poorest-performing sector, for the reasons noted previously. </FONT></P>

Over the long run, a prudent, balanced approach allows you to participate in the markets&#146; gains while cushioning the effects of the markets&#146; darker days. </FONT></P>
